A fresh agent costs more than it looks. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your one lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. - **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Documentation

Taskflow keeps three kinds of document under `docs/`. They do not carry equal weight.

| Folder | What it is | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/adr/` | Architecture Decision Records: numbered, dated, reviewed. | **Authoritative.** |
| `docs/product/` | Product notes written before or alongside a feature: intent, examples, wording. | Context only. |
| `docs/support/` | Runbooks and support macros: what people observed. | Describes behaviour, never specifies it. |

## Precedence

1. An ADR is the specification for every question it addresses. The highest-numbered ADR that addresses a question is the one that applies; a later ADR supersedes an earlier one only where it says so.
2. Where a product note and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins. A product note that predates an ADR on the same subject is kept for history, not as a second opinion.
3. Support notes record what was seen at the time. They are never evidence of intended behaviour.
4. Code comments, `TODO`s and function names are not documentation. They are frequently stale.
5. Where no document speaks, the current behaviour of the code is authoritative, and a new feature follows the conventions of its sibling features (same error classes, same guards, same events).
# ADR 0012 — Cloning a project

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-03-25
- Supersedes: `docs/product/project-clone-notes.md` where the two disagree.

## Context

Teams run the same shape of project repeatedly (a release train, an onboarding checklist) and
want to start the next one from the last. The product wants a "clone project" action that
creates a new project from an existing one, optionally with its issues. Issues are numbered per
project, counted per project against the plan, indexed for search and metered for usage, so a
clone is a batch of creations and has to behave like one. This record fixes what is copied,
what is reset, and how the batch is gated.

## Decision

1. **The clone is a new project of the same workspace**, with the name, slug and key the caller
   chose. Its description, visibility, colour and lead are copied from the source. It starts
   `active`, with no start or target date, and it is not archived. The slug is treated exactly
   like a created project's slug (made unique by suffix when taken). The key is the caller's
   responsibility.

2. **Gates, like a creation.** Cloning needs the permission to read the source project and the
   permission to create a project, both checked against the acting member. The source must be a
   live project of the workspace. The plan's project quota applies as it does to creating a
   project.

3. **A clone is a fresh start.** When issues are included, every **live** (not archived) issue of
   the source is copied; archived issues are not. Each copy keeps the source issue's title,
   description, priority, estimate, due date and labels. Everything that records progress is
   reset: the copy starts in the workspace's default issue status, unassigned, with no start or
   completion time, authored by the person cloning. Comments and attachments are not copied,
   and whatever an issue is linked to is not copied either.

4. **Numbering.** The copies are numbered from 1 in the order of the source issues' numbers, so
   the clone reads in the same order as the source; issues created in the clone afterwards
   continue after them.

5. **All or nothing.** The clone is checked before anything is written: the plan's per-project
   issue quota applies to the whole batch of copies (as many issues as would be copied, counted
   the way a single creation counts them). If the batch does not fit, the clone is refused and
   nothing is created — no project, no issues.

6. **Announcing.** A clone publishes exactly one domain event, `project.cloned`, and records one
   audit entry under the new project. It does not publish `project.created` or one
   `issue.created` per copy. The things those announcements would have driven still happen:
   the clone and its issues are searchable at once, and the workspace's project and issue
   meters reflect the clone at once.

## Consequences

- Copying must walk every live issue of the source, however many there are; a page is not a
  project.
- Whatever the copier borrows, a copy never keeps the source row's status, assignee or number
  (rules 3 and 4).
# Cloning a project — product notes

_Written while scoping the "duplicate project" action (2026-01). Kept for history; see `docs/adr/0012-cloning-a-project.md` for the current rules._

## Why

Release trains and onboarding checklists are the same project over and over. People want
"duplicate" on the project page.

## What we'd like

- A "Duplicate project…" entry asking for a name; the slug and key are derived from it.
- Everything comes along: the issues with their status and assignee, so the board of the copy
  looks exactly like the board of the original; archived issues too, so the history is complete.
- Issue numbers are kept, so cross-references in descriptions ("see PLAT-12") still make sense
  in the copy.
- Comments are not copied (they are conversations, not work).
- The copy is announced like any new project, and each copied issue like any new issue, so the
  people assigned to them hear about it.

## Open questions

- Plan limits: a copy of a big project could blow the per-project issue limit. Leaning towards
  copying as many as fit and telling the user.

content.text:
`cloneProject` is built to ADR 0012, which overrides the product notes where they disagree. The full suite passes (637 tests, 20 of them new), and `tsc` and `eslint` are clean. No existing test needed changing, because none encoded behaviour this change alters.

**The four exports**
- **Schema:** `cloneProjectSchema` and `CloneProjectInput` are in `src/schemas/project.ts`.
- **Service:** `cloneProject(actor, input)` is in `project-service.ts` and returns the new project as stored.
- **Event:** `project.cloned` is in `TaskflowEventMap` and is published once, with the cloning member as actor.
- **Audit action:** `project.cloned` is on the audit type, the audit-filter zod schema, the activity label map and the activity listener (subject and project id are the new project, metadata `{ sourceProjectId, issuesCopied }`).

**What the clone does**
- **Gates:** the source must be a live project of the workspace, and the actor needs `project:read` on it and `project:create`. The project quota uses the same count and message as `createProject`.
- **Issue quota:** it applies to the whole batch of copies. A refused clone writes nothing, and a batch that exactly fills the quota is accepted.
- **Project:** it keeps the source's description, visibility, colour and lead, starts `active` with no dates, and is not archived. The caller's slug is made unique by suffix when taken, and the key is used as given.
- **Issues:** all live issues are copied, not just the first page (a test clones 130). Archived issues are not copied. Copies keep title, description, priority, estimate, due date and labels. They start in the workspace's default status, unassigned, authored by the actor, with no start or completion time and no parent. They are numbered from 1 in the source's number order.
- **Not copied:** comments and attachments.
- **Atomic write:** the project and its issues are written in one transaction (`insertProjectClone` in `project-repository.ts`), so a failure part-way leaves nothing behind. The key is not checked for uniqueness, so a key that already exists makes the insert fail, nothing is written, and the caller gets the raw database error.
- **Announcing:** the clone publishes only `project.cloned` (no `project.created`, no `issue.created`). Because those events normally drive search indexing and the usage meters, `cloneProject` updates both directly. The audit entry comes from the activity listener on `project.cloned`.

I did not use the ops console's `duplicateProject` / `copyIssuesToProject`: they skip the gates, keep status, assignee and numbers, and copy only the first 100 issues. I left them as they were, and added `listLiveIssuesForClone` in `issue-repository.ts` to read the whole source.

The new tests are in `tests/services/project-service.clone.test.ts`, plus additions to `tests/schemas/project.schema.test.ts`.

If the search indexing or meter update fails after the clone has been written, `cloneProject` throws even though the clone exists and `project.cloned` has already been published. The event bus normally isolates failures like that; I didn't replicate that isolation here.
